title: Symmetric Matrices: LDL^T and Cholesky
quickIdea: A symmetric matrix factors as L D L^T with the same L on both sides; when the pivots are positive you can take square roots and get the Cholesky factor C with A = C C^T.
remember: Symmetry survives only in the LDL^T form. The plain L and U of a symmetric matrix are generally not symmetric - a lower triangular matrix equal to its transpose is diagonal.
D is the diagonal of the pivots, so A = L D L^T with L unit lower triangular.
If A is symmetric positive definite, every pivot is positive, and C = L diag(sqrt(d1), ..., sqrt(dn)) satisfies A = C C^T.
The 2x2 test for positive definiteness is a11 > 0 and det(A) > 0.
Cholesky needs about half the storage and half the work of LU, because only one triangle has to be kept.

example.prompt: Factor A = [[4,2],[2,3]] as LDL^T and as C C^T.
example.work: Doolittle gives L = [[1,0],[1/2,1]] and U = [[4,2],[0,2]], so D = diag(4,2). Scaling each column of L by the square root of its pivot gives C = [[2,0],[1,sqrt2]].

gateAngle: Cholesky is outside the three words of the syllabus line, so this card is P3. But option 4 of GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.34 tests precisely the fact that a symmetric P does not give symmetric L and U, and the correct thing to say instead is that it gives LDL^T. That makes this the one card in the topic that answers a wrong option in a real question.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Is A = [[1,2],[2,5]] positive definite, and what is its Cholesky factor?
variations.why: The pivots are 1 and 1, both positive, so both square roots are real; the factor is read off in the same two steps as an LU factorization.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why must every pivot be positive for Cholesky to exist, when LU only needs them nonzero?
variations.answer: Because Cholesky takes the square root of each pivot, which is real only when the pivot is positive. A negative pivot gives a valid LU factorization but no real C.
variations.why: Positive definiteness is exactly the condition that makes all pivots positive, which is why the two notions coincide.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A symmetric 3x3 has pivots 2, -1 and 4. Which of LDL^T and Cholesky exist?
variations.answer: LDL^T exists with D = diag(2,-1,4); Cholesky does not, because the second pivot is negative and has no real square root.
variations.why: The sign of the pivots is what separates the two factorizations, and a negative pivot means the matrix is indefinite rather than positive definite.

trap.what: Concluding that a symmetric matrix has symmetric L and U.
trap.why: L is lower triangular and U is upper triangular, so for either to equal its transpose it would have to be diagonal; a unit diagonal then forces L = I, which would make A = U upper triangular as well as symmetric, hence diagonal.
trap.counterexample: P = [[1,2,0],[2,5,1],[0,1,3]] is symmetric, and its Doolittle factors are L = [[1,0,0],[2,1,0],[0,1,1]] and U = [[1,2,0],[0,1,1],[0,0,2]]. Neither is symmetric, which is why statement 4 of GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.34 is false.

check.question: For A = [[4,2],[2,3]], what is D, and what are the entries of C on its diagonal?
check.answer: D = diag(4,2) and C's diagonal is (2, sqrt2).
check.explanation: Each diagonal entry of C is the square root of the matching pivot, which is why positive definiteness is needed: here both pivots are positive.
